title: Guests at Mamre and a Plea for Sodom
summary: Three visitors come to Abraham's tent at midday, and he welcomes them with lavish hospitality. One of them, the LORD, promises that Sarah will have a son within a year; Sarah, listening inside the tent, laughs. As the visitors set out toward Sodom, the LORD reveals that he will investigate its outcry, and Abraham intercedes, bargaining from fifty righteous people down to ten.
story: Genesis 17 ended with the covenant sign and the promise of Isaac within a year. Now the promise comes in person, at Abraham's own table, and Sarah hears it for herself. The second half of the chapter turns toward Sodom, where Lot has settled (Genesis 13:12-13). Abraham, who once rescued Lot with a sword (Genesis 14), now pleads for the city with words. The chapter joins two things that run through the rest of Scripture: God's promise to bless Abraham's family, and God's intention that through that family the nations would be blessed, including by the prayers of the one he has chosen.
historical:
The scene is set at the great trees of Mamre, near Hebron in the hill country south of Jerusalem, where Abraham had settled (Genesis 13:18) and where he would later bury Sarah (Genesis 23:19). The site was remembered for centuries. A large stone enclosure was built at the traditional location, Ramat el-Khalil north of Hebron, in the Herodian period, and the emperor Constantine had a church built there in the fourth century AD. None of that proves where the original oaks stood, but it shows how long the memory of this meeting was honored.

Sodom and Gomorrah lay in the region of the Jordan valley and the Dead Sea (Genesis 13:10-12). Their exact sites are uncertain and are discussed in the note on Genesis 19.
cultural:
Abraham's hospitality follows the code of the ancient Near East, especially among those who lived in tents. A traveler at midday, in the heat, was a guest to be protected and fed, and the host's honor depended on it. Abraham runs, bows, offers a little water and a bit of bread, and then serves a feast: three seahs of fine flour (a very large quantity, far more than three guests could eat), a choice calf (meat was rarely eaten and marked a special occasion), curds, and milk. Modest words and lavish action were the polite form. He stands by them as they eat, taking the posture of a servant.

The detail matters because the next chapter shows the opposite. Lot will also welcome guests, but the men of Sodom will try to violate them. Hospitality becomes a measure of righteousness, and Hebrews 13:2 later recalls this scene in urging Christians to welcome strangers, since some have entertained angels without knowing it.
literary: The chapter has two movements joined by a walk. In the first (verses 1-15), the narrator tells us at once that “the LORD appeared to Abraham,” while Abraham sees only three men; the reader knows more than he does. The identity of the visitor comes into focus slowly, until “the LORD” speaks directly to Sarah's hidden laughter. In the second (verses 16-33), God speaks to himself (“Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?”) before inviting Abraham into his counsel. Abraham's intercession follows a strict descending pattern, fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten, each time with deeper humility (“I am but dust and ashes”), and each time God grants the request. The dialogue stops at ten; Abraham stops asking, not God.

outline.t: Abraham welcomes three visitors at Mamre
The promise of a son and Sarah's laughter
The LORD reveals his purpose concerning Sodom
Abraham pleads for the righteous in the city

doctrines.note: Abraham's intercession is bold, persistent, and humble at once. He appeals to God's own character (“Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?”), and God welcomes the appeal. God chooses to take his friend into his counsel and to act in response to prayer.

God's judgment is not arbitrary. He goes down to see whether the outcry is true before acting, and he is willing to spare a whole city for the sake of a few righteous people. Judgment in Scripture is the response of a just God to real wrong.

“Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” (verse 14) sets God's power against the plain facts of old age. The same chapter shows his justice and patience. Power, justice, and mercy are held together, not traded against one another.

words.note: Pala, to be wonderful, extraordinary, or beyond someone's power. In verse 14 the question is literally whether anything is too wonderful for the LORD. The related noun describes God's wonders in the exodus. The word marks what lies beyond human ability but not beyond God's.

Za'aqah, outcry: the cry of the oppressed calling for help or justice. The related verb describes Israel crying out under slavery in Egypt (Exodus 2:23). The outcry against Sodom suggests victims crying out, which Ezekiel 16:49 later connects with arrogance, excess, and neglect of the poor and needy.

Mishpat, justice: right judgment, and the order that results from it. In verse 19 God chooses Abraham so that his household will keep the way of the LORD by doing “what is right and just.” Abraham appeals to the same quality in God: the Judge of all the earth must do mishpat.

christ: When the angel Gabriel tells Mary that her relative Elizabeth, old and barren, has conceived, he says that nothing is impossible with God (Luke 1:37), wording that closely echoes the Greek translation of Genesis 18:14. The God who gave a son to Sarah gives a son to a virgin. The promise of verse 18, that through Abraham “all the nations of the earth will be blessed”, is read by Paul as the gospel announced in advance (Galatians 3:8). Abraham's intercession for the city is a pattern that finds its fullness in Christ, who lives to intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25). Abraham asked that the righteous not die with the wicked; the gospel goes further, declaring that the Righteous One died for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18). That last link is thematic rather than a direct New Testament use of this chapter. Many Christians have also read the three visitors in light of the Trinity, as in Andrei Rublev's fifteenth-century icon, though the text itself presents the LORD accompanied by two others who in the next chapter are called angels.

hard.q: Did God need to “go down to see” Sodom, and did Abraham change God's mind?
hard.a:
Verse 21 speaks of God going down to find out whether the outcry is true, and the dialogue that follows reads like a negotiation. Most interpreters understand the first as the language of a just judge: God doesn't need information, but Scripture pictures him investigating before he judges, so that no one can accuse him of acting on hearsay. Genesis 11:5 uses the same picture at Babel.

On the second question, Christians hold a range of views. The classical view holds that God knows the end from the beginning and does not change, and that prayer is one of the means by which he has chosen to carry out his purposes; Abraham's pleading is real, and it is also what God was drawing out of him by revealing his plan (verse 17). Some theologians stress God's genuine responsiveness and give more weight to the language of relationship and give-and-take. All agree that God invites his people to plead with him on the basis of his own character, and that he is more merciful than Abraham dares to ask.

questions: Abraham gave strangers his best without knowing who they were. What would it look like to practice that kind of welcome now?
Sarah laughed because the promise seemed impossible. Where do you find it hardest to believe that anything is too difficult for the LORD?
Abraham prayed boldly for a city that wasn't his own. Who or what might God be inviting you to pray for with that kind of persistence?
